The main purpose of this PR is easing the migration from .NET Framework to .NET. We're implemeting some features to increase the compat.

issue_context.title: `HttpWebRequest.AllowWriteStreamBuffering` seems to lack an implementation
issue_context.body:
### Description

There is a properly on `HttpWebRequest` called `AllowWriteStreamBuffering`. However, setting it doesn't seem to have any effect; the request body is still buffered to a `MemoryStream` before the request is sent. This makes it rather difficult to do things like upload massive files via HTTP PUT or POST.

The following comment seems to indicate that the functionality of unbuffered write streams, as originally implemented in the .NET Framework, was torn out of the code as part of .NET Core development because .NET Core's `HttpWebRequest` lacked an `AllowWriteStreamBuffering`:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/56135728983a635dad49441728d2c30e200eb575/src/libraries/System.Net.Requests/src/System/Net/RequestStream.cs#L11-L15

...and then it was never reintroduced, even though the property was reintroduced in .NET Core 2.0 (according to the documentation).

In my testing, running against .NET 5.0, extremely large files cannot be transferred at all, because regardless of the value of `AllowWriteStreamBuffering`, trying to write them to the request body stream produces the following exception:
```
System.IO.IOException: Stream was too long.
```
This is an exception produced by the `MemoryStream` class.

### Reproduction Steps

```
			var request = (HttpWebRequest)WebRequest.Create("https://google.com/test"); // exact URL is irrelevant because request never gets that far

			request.AllowWriteStreamBuffering = false;
			request.Method = "PUT";

			using (var requestStream = request.GetRequestStream())
			{
				byte[] buffer = new byte[1048576];

				for (int megabyte = 0; megabyte < 2048; megabyte++)
					requestStream.Write(buffer, 0, buffer.Length);
			}
```

### Expected behavior

The above sample should actually connect to Google and try to send 2 GB of zeroes (don't do this :-) ).

### Actual behavior

No connection at all is made because `GetRequestStream` actually just creates a `MemoryStream` under the hood to buffer the full request body, even though `AllowWriteStreamBuffering` is `false`.

### Regression?

I am reasonably confident that this code works properly in the full .NET Framework right up to version 4.8.

### Known Workarounds

_No response_

### Configuration

I need to run more testing to confirm, but I believe the bug reproduces on all .NET Core versions, as well as .NET 5.0 and .NET 6 prereleases. The bug does not reproduce on any .NET Framework version, right up to 4.8.

### Other information

_No response_

I'm confused -- isn't `HttpClient` built on top of `HttpWebRequest`??

> I'm confused -- isn't HttpClient built on top of HttpWebRequest??

In .NET Core, it's the other way around.

Huh, okay. Doesn't that then mean that if you want to write code that works on both platforms, you have to have per-framework implementations, because on .NET Framework, using `HttpClient` is going to use `HttpWebRequest` in a way that buffers, while on .NET Core, using `HttpWebRequest` is going to buffer the data before passing it off to `HttpClient`? 🤔
You should be using HttpClient on both .NET Framework and .NET Core (you can control the buffering behavior using HttpClient in both cases).

Okay :-) In that case, while it is a real issue, it isn't an issue causing me problems. I have confirmed that an `HttpClient`-based implementation does not exhibit the pathological buffering on .NET Core.

review_comments:
This is leaving an unobserved exception.

Can we add something like
```c#
await Assert.ThrowsAnyAsync<Exception>(() => request.GetResponseAsync());
```

How are we making sure that in case of `buffering` this is not getting buffered before sending?
For example, could we somehow make sure that the server received some request content before we finished sending all of it?
Yes, I can write a test for it with a raw `Socket`, instead of using the `HttpServer`.

You don't have to write raw socket test. LoopbackServer has individual functions/helper to read headers and body, even to read a block of bytes:
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/bd5f6eb73f6dffe91386f75d3ed5531ddcb2aeb6/src/libraries/Common/tests/System/Net/Http/LoopbackServer.cs#L543-L543
Should you set `_disposed = true` here as well?
I'll not push on this suggestion, but you could use this to actually return the length when you know it because you're buffering.
Since I've separated streams this is not needed anymore.
Why doesn't this class `Dispose` dispose the `MemoryStream`?
Because user will be controlling this class and they can choose to dispose it before we send the request (Before calling `GetResponse`), in that case we'll try to use disposed `MemoryStream`

> they can choose to dispose it before we send the request (Before calling GetResponse)

Is this a valid use that is expected to work? Are you saying that this sequence of actions work on Framework?
Are we intentionally disposing the stream before getting the response? Can't this result in a race?

> Can't this result in a race?

Which scenario do you have in your mind?

> Are we intentionally disposing the stream before getting the response?

Yes, because either disposing of the stream or calling the `GetResponse` will cause `EndWrite` on `StreamBuffer`, and the request itself will be sent, and we're going to capture the result from a `Task`.
